az_moby_dick.notes: Start at the double crack left of the giant flake. Climb right of two thin cracks until they split, follow the left fork to cruxy face moves past one bolt, then easier face climbing to a two-bolt belay. Length is estimated.

Step left to an exposed arete and climb up and right past a short system of parallel cracks, then up and right over face and chickenheads, arching left to a comfortable ledge with a small pine tree. Some parties continue about 20 ft to a belay on large chickenheads.

Continue up the face left of the large flake, past one bolt, for about 160 ft to a belay on an obvious sea of chickenheads. Slings and runners on the knobs make good gear and anchors. Length is estimated.
Climb the remaining chickenheads to a bolted move over a large flake or corner, then up and right past another bolt and over a blocky lip to a two-bolt belay on a ledge.
Extremely fun climbing over a sea of chickenheads, past two bolts, to a large toothy dike where you can belay, or continue about 30 ft of slab to a belay in an obvious seam.
A sixth short stretch of fourth-class slabbing, 100 to 200 ft, leads to the summit. Many parties count the climb as five pitches.

nv_epinephrine.notes: Leave the creek bed and clip bolts up to a large ledge, then a few more bolts lead on to a ledge with bushes, about 165 ft.
Head up and left into a chimney, exit on its right, and follow easier ground to the foot of the large chimney on the right flank of the Black Tower. A long pitch; the rope may need to stretch.

The centrepiece: a smooth, wide crack climbed as a chimney, well protected, for about 140 ft to a bolted station on a ledge on the right-hand wall. Haul the pack on a long sling through the chimneys instead of wearing it.

Chimney higher, moving left where the crack pinches down, then easier ground to a ledge. Beyond it a slimmer chimney starts at a fixed nut and has two bolts that are easy to miss; climb out from the chimney's back to spot them. If the rope reaches, belay on top of the Black Tower; if not, stop where the chimney ends and add a short, easy pitch to the top of the tower. The bottom of the chimney can be bypassed to the right.
Above the tower's top, take the face through an overhang and head for a ledge with brush on it.
Traverse easily right to the Elephant's Trunk and climb it to a ledge at its top.
Climb the crack, with a few bolts along it, to a bolted station on a ledge. Rappels descend directly below this point. It can be linked with the previous pitch.

Stay in the same crack for about 400 ft in all, belaying at each bolted station. On pitch 10, traverse a short way right past a bolt to a small roof, then a second roof that is a bit harder; protection is good and there are big holds above and to the left of the crack. Some of the finest climbing on the route.

or_wherever_i_may_roam.notes: Knobby climbing up past several bolts to the top of a pillar, where the belay is. Getting started off the ground is the hardest part.
Step across the gap from the pillar onto the main wall. The crux comes in the first few bolts; reports place it either below the second bolt or past the third. Belay on a ledge.
A very airy traverse over to the third anchors, about 60 ft, ending at the base of an arete. Pitches 2 and 3 link well, which keeps the leader in sight of the belayer.
A few exciting moves up the arete, then veer right and follow an edge with the ground dropping away below. Often called the hardest pitch of the route.
Easy greenish slab (about 5.4) toward a short headwall; the headwall is rated 5.8 by one account and the pitch is easier than the ones below. Pitches 4 and 5 can be linked with a 70 m rope.

ut_finger_of_fate.notes: Start in the crack system about 30 ft left of the descent gully. Aid the crack past a false belay to the real one, roughly 130 ft up. Much of it would go free at a moderate grade. If aiding without back-cleaning, carry three each of #2 and #3 and two #4s.
Stay in the crack as it opens into a flared groove.
Follow the clear line up to a ledge where the Finger begins. Right off the belay, old pin scars and holes give short but tricky aid, and some free moves are mandatory and committing.

Traverse the ledge around the corner (about 5.6) to an ancient bolt, aid the tricky roof (about A2), and continue to a belay on the far side of the Finger. The traverse is protected by old drilled angles and a star drive; fixed tricams and fixed pins at the start of the roof are old and sketchy. A screamer helps for anchor falls. This gets you to the base of the Finger.
Scramble to a drilled pin, then climb the strenuous flare (aid C1, or free about 5.10). At its top, 5.8 grovelling is needed to reach the belay, which is on the ridge facing the Duck.
Go around the Duck on its left. The anchor for the descent rappels is on its far side. Keep following the wide cracks up to a big ledge, which is a bivy site, and belay there.

Move right around the arete to a seam and aid it (about A2) back to the crest. A mix of free climbing (5.7-5.8) and C2 aid on doubtful fixed gear reaches an exposed stance on the arete; placements and a fixed pin lead to many bolts to anchor.

Mixed free (5.7-5.8) and aid (C2, long reaches) past old fixed gear to a wide crack. Continue up it, over a roof in the caprock with wild exposure, and mantle to the belay. Nearly a bolt ladder, with free moves and top steps.

ut_prodigal_sun.notes: Two pitches usually led as one, roughly 160 ft. The opening bolt sits around nine feet up, so bring a stick-clip or a boost.
About 70 ft to a comfortable ledge, a usual place to stop for the night when fixing the lower pitches.
The Wrinkles. Pendulum out to the right and tension traverse back to the left in a series; once the good placements end, head left. This is the hardest aid of the route.
A good crack leads through the arching roof.
Follow a crack to a short bolt ladder.
A left-facing corner with a few trickier moves, ending at a decent stance below the last aid pitch. Tricam placements between bolt ladders on the upper pitches have flared out and held poorly.
Continue up the corner system, then pendulum left into another corner. The pitch ends on a large, dirty, sandy, down-sloping ledge with loose material, so move carefully.
Free climb a low-angle chimney full of loose debris, then a chute of loose sand, rock and plant matter. The belay is at a pair of good trees.

wa_action_potential.notes: A fun flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left; the scramble concludes at a horn wrapped in fixed webbing.
Step left to a sweet, right-trending finger crack; pull a bulge and cut hard left to a stance.
The steepest pitch: a lichen-covered finger crack up spooky flakes to a good belay ledge.
Trend left toward the chimney and belay on its left side.
A fun, mostly solid chimney; the blocks are generally sound but warrant care.
Poorer-quality rock requiring a left traverse to a right-facing corner.
Steep bulges with just enough gear to feel heads-up in the mid-5.10 range; belay beyond the arête.
Rambling terrain, up to 5.7, to the skyline and true summit, or finish by traversing Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.notes: A steep corner just left of the crest; feels closer to 5.9+ with a heavy pack.
Fun, moderate climbing directly on the buttress crest.
Steep rock left of the crest to the ledge used by Beckey and Fielding as a bivy on the first ascent, leading into an off-width crack.
The technical crux: an off-width crack with surprisingly positive, crimpy holds; an easier 5.8 alternative exists via the buttress crest.
Blocks and cracks on the crest continuing to the base of a steep step.
Airy, exhilarating face climbing directly on the crest with perfectly positioned holds; an easier tension-traverse alternative exists.
Blocky climbing to the top of the buttress, from where it's a scramble to the true summit.

wa_beckey_davis.notes: Climb the left-side chimney between two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; move left atop the chimney onto knobby terrain to belay.
Sustained knobby face, slabs, and cracks up toward a gully/chimney system; route-finding is somewhat ambiguous through this stretch on the way to Snafflehound Ledge.
Traverse right across the obvious Snafflehound Ledge to a small tree, then a short steep step to the base of the crux pitch.
Route crux: a shallow left-facing dihedral forces you right until an overhang forces a step-across left into a flaring jam crack; eases above the bulge on face holds and chicken-heads.
Crack system/steep gully bypassing a chockstone on the left to the small notch east of the summit horn; watch for loose blocks in the gully.

Delicate friction traverse on a ramp finishing on a good jam crack to the summit; a harder 5.10a thin-hands splitter variant climbs straight out of the notch for parties wanting more technical finish.

wa_big_kangaroo_west_face.notes: Starts in the shallow gully beneath the route's distinctive chockstone, then climbs an easy low-5th slab protected by small gear up to a sling belay.

Traverses toward the summit block, skirting it on the left via a narrow horizontal foot-ledge over growing exposure; about 15 feet in, a large flake takes a 1-2" cam before a low-5th step around it to the next stance.

Beautiful compact granite with decent edges and side-pulls for about 20 feet to the first gear in a crack, then a steep move past a single old, rusty 1/4-inch bolt to the tiny summit — essentially unprotected and the crux of the whole route; downclimbed or top-roped back to the belay rather than rappelled since there's no real anchor at the top.
wa_big_kangaroo_west_face.anchor: Walk-off / top-rope off summit bolt (no real rap anchor)

wa_bobcat_cringe.notes: Start as for Peanuts, then cut right on easy ground to a 2-bolt belay.
Crux pitch; thin splitter crack past 2 bolts and 1 fixed pin to chains; thin laybacking, pocket pulling, tip-jamming, knob climbing.

wa_bonanza_peak_cascadian_route.notes: Easy climbing up pale slabs to a comfortable stance beneath a darker band of rock. Treat it as a warm-up and a chance to sort out the rope.
Follow an open book to its top, then move left across low-fifth-class ground to a talus-strewn bowl where the belay sits.
Take the rib on the right side of the bowl, with some scrambling mixed in, to a wide talus ledge. A long lead, so expect rope drag.

Crosses a very loose band of rock before reaching a gully with sounder stone. Little reliable protection and a lot of loose material; keep the second clear of the fall line. A weathered old cam was found around here, hinting at an earlier attempt.
Easy fifth-class going up the gully, ending at a secure belay.
More of the same gully, easy fifth-class ground.
Angle left to a left-facing corner and climb it to a good ledge on the prow.
Climb past one roof, up a ramp, and on to a second roof. A good ledge above serves as the belay.
A thin right-facing corner, then a short steep section, a ramp and a further corner lead to a big ledge.
Low-angle but loose face climbing ending at a poor belay.
Face climbing to a reasonable ledge; the anchor there takes some care to build. Run-out in places.
Keeps going up the face, finishing in the notch where the ridge shoulders out. Also run-out in places.
A short overhanging splitter crack, the hardest climbing on the route by grade, finishing on a loose ramp.
A varnished corner that relaxes into loose, mid-fifth-class terrain.
Traverse right to a ramp and follow it to the south ridge.

wa_boving_roofs.notes: A short, loose approach pitch off the shared Southwest Rib start, climbing blocky, sometimes-loose ground up to a belay stance directly beneath the two roofs.
The 'money pitch': sustained, powerful climbing under and through the striking double roof, protecting well with 0.5-3in cams. Watch for a loose block right at the start.
Starts up an easy chimney that steepens into sustained 5.9 thin-hands, then steps right to top out at the head of the Southwest Rib's Bear Hug pitch.

wa_chair_peak_voie_de_chaise.notes: The hardest moves come right off the ground, a few tricky 5.7 steps onto the slab; after that the pitch settles into sustained, clean 5.6 slab on solid rock with bolts throughout. The P1 anchor is also the last rappel station, and a rap from it drops straight down rather than back to the true base.

Three distinct sections: an awkward 5.8 move over an overlap, an easy left-facing corner, then a steeper 5.8 finish. Put a long sling on the bolt before the line trends right, or rope drag builds quickly.

Head right off the belay, passing a rappel station on the way, then make a few insecure slab moves up through a series of small overlaps (5.7). Easier slab leads to the next anchor; do not confuse the passed rap station with the P3 belay.

A lower-angle pitch of mostly moderate climbing that ends on a flat ledge nicknamed the Heli pad, directly beneath the steep band that holds the crux. Get comfortable here; the next pitch starts steep straight off the belay.

The crux, known as the 30 Seconds Out pitch. Step right off the belay and aim for the weakness marked by a small but obvious triangular roof, then work through it with laybacks and high steps. Short but steep, and some moves feel committing between bolts.

Easy climbing up and left, then straight up, but this is where the rock quality drops: the pitch is dirty and holds loose stones, so clear debris only when no party is below. Belay at the anchor without chains; the chained anchor off to the right is a rappel station.
A lower-angle 5.6 slab to the last bolted belay. Rock remains looser than on the lower pitches, so move carefully and watch for anything dislodged by the rope.

Follow a faint path a few feet left, then cut back right on a faint trail beneath a small slab protected by three bolts (3rd–4th class). A belay at a tree with a webbing anchor precedes the climbers' trail that trends right to the summit ridge. Belay back down this section on descent rather than rappelling it, which knocks loose rock onto parties below.

wa_concord_tower_north_face.notes: Short pitch off the notch up an obvious crack system to a big ledge dotted with small trees — over quickly, a good warm-up for the harder climbing above.

The route's crux: pull onto hollow, flaky-sounding rock and jam through pockets and huecos, including a 10-15 ft unprotectable blank section that climbs easier than it looks thanks to huge hueco jugs. Stay left here — angling right past this point puts you on the neighboring Tunnel Route by mistake.

Head left up crack systems, cross two low-angle 5.0 slabs, and mantle a bear-hug flake to gain the small, exposed summit — the final move onto the block is tricky enough that most leaders place one more piece before topping out.

wa_crying_dragon.notes: The start of the Davis-Holland: hand and finger jamming in a crack that is sometimes wet when the rest of the wall is dry. Belay at two bolts on a good ledge. The same pitch is given as 5.8+ elsewhere.

Continue up the Davis-Holland: fingers and thin hands in a right-facing corner to a two-bolt anchor on a sloping ledge. This is the most gear-hungry pitch. With some backcleaning it links with the next pitch into one long 55 m pitch of 5.10.

Look up and right for a lone black-hangered bolt. Undercling the roof as for the right variation of Davis-Holland, reach a jug under the bolt, then a short tricky section (horizontal takes a #2 Camalot) leads onto the second pitch of Rise and Fall. Skip the belay out right, clip the next black bolt up-left, and follow crystal edges up a dike; the crux is getting past two roofs at the end. Three-bolt belay.

Up Rise and Fall past one bolt to a finger crack, then step right to a Green Drag-on bolt and up to its hanging anchor under a roof. Clip it as protection, make a hard move into the steep crack exiting the right side of the roof, and follow sustained 5.10 crack to a two-bolt stance on the left. That anchor is not set up for rappel.

Up the corner on thin gear to a good jug, then clip the shiny bolt out right (the bolts up and left belong to Green Drag-on). A balancy section leads to a tenuous second clip, then powerful moves work right past the third bolt to the three-bolt Town Crier anchor. Bouldery and fun.

Up the Town Crier flare past fixed pins (back them up with thin gear), then a layback crux gets you onto a flexy flake; two bolts protect. Traverse left immediately along the horizontal crack; going straight up is the much harder Town Crier crux. Jugs lead back to Green Drag-on and its final 5.10 crack to an anchor on a busy ledge. A #3 is useful here.

wa_davis_holland_route.notes: Jam the hand crack at the far left of the upper walls, where the approach trail arrives. It is often damp even when the rest of the route is dry; stemming off the left wall helps on the slippery opening layback. From the ledge, wander right and then back left over small terraces to a bolted belay in a right-facing corner.

Jam and layback the crack in the right-facing corner to the next bolted belay. It is a sustained, pumpy fingers-to-thin-hands crack that takes #0.75 Camalots nearly the whole way, so bring several; larger hands find it harder. Voices do not carry well between this belay and the next.

Make a bouldery move up and right around the roof, then back left into a right-facing corner; a variation goes directly left past a bolt on balancy friction that may be harder. The crux is in the corner, on delicate footwork and small edges protected by small nuts, so carry extras. It ends at a bolted ledge where most parties rappel or continue up Lovin' Arms.

wa_direct_west_face.notes: Starts just left of the toe of the face in an obvious corner: hand cracks and a corner on dark, solid rock up to slabs beneath the big wave-shaped roof.
A thin crack and slab angle up and right to a belay directly under the roof.
The crux: traverse left on slabs around the roof, then climb a steep corner with an off-fingers crack and a bulge, with stemming, finishing left into a seam and grooves. A full 60 m pitch.
Step left across a slab into more cracks; intermittent finger cracks run a full rope length between a corner and a large freestanding horn.
A committing move off the belay, then an arching corner with a thin finger crack under its lip; pull over the lip onto roughly 30 ft of runout face and slab.
Broken face through a small notch, then left onto good cracks.
A crack that seams out briefly leads to the ridge crest. The narrow crest does not connect to the summit; a fixed nut anchor there serves a 60 m rappel to sandy benches below.
wa_direct_west_face.anchor: Fixed nut rappel anchor on the ridge crest

wa_direct_west_face.notes: From the benches, a 5.10 corner leads to the summit block, which is climbed on two old aid bolts — one without a hanger, the other loose in its hole.

wa_dirty_sanchez.notes: The route begins on the second obvious rib, not the first, below a huge tree that marks the top of pitch 1. Scramble loose ground from the base to a small tree and belay there; the rib is easy to misidentify, so look for the big tree above before starting.

Face and mossy slab up and right on flakes to the route's only bolt on this pitch, just below a huge tree. The tree is too thick for a short cordelette — bring a long sling or about 10 ft of cord to go around it. Given as 5.3-5.4.

Climb up and right to a left-facing corner on small ledges; the bolts are close together low and spread out near the top, where small gear (under 3/4 inch) can supplement them. Ends at a two-bolt anchor.

Follow a right-facing corner to a crack/face feature that can be face-climbed on the left or jammed on the right. Many of the cracks are small, dirty or flaring gaps between detached blocks, so good placements take searching. Top out on the corner to a two-bolt anchor in a left-facing corner.

Follow a left-facing corner on relatively good rock until it fades about 80 ft up, then look immediately right for a three-bolt anchor — it sits just before the half-rope mark on a 60 m rope and is easy to climb past.

Leave the anchor with scarce protection straight up toward a prominent right-facing corner; one bolt protects the moves into a tricky notch, then jam the corner as it narrows to a finger crack. Lichen and smeary feet make it feel harder than 5.7. Build a gear anchor in the deep notch; the blocks there need care.
Short, steep face past four bolts to a two-bolt anchor. The clips above the first bolt are awkward, and holds here can break off — test everything and keep your belayer out of the fall line.

The Jenga Traverse: cross an exposed knife-edge with little or no protection (a projecting block about halfway can be slung), then climb up through loose blocks and rubble. Place a couple of solid pieces just before topping out and finish at a single bolt; back it up with gear. Easy climbing, but the protection and rock make it feel much harder than 5.5.

wa_east_face_6.notes: A vegetated, lichen-encrusted low-fifth-class chimney off the broad heather ledge system.
A short traverse across a small heathered ledge into an exposed, pleasant fourth-class face.
An obvious deep low-fifth-class chimney that tops out just a few feet from the summit cairn.

wa_easy_getaway.notes: 100 ft right-facing corner (RFC) that varies hands to fingers - very secure but sustained; the highlight pitch of the route.

wa_ellation.notes: Start in the series of shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, marked by a bolt near the ground. Climb the bolted groove to a spacious tree ledge. Dirt washes onto this pitch from the ledge above, so expect it to be a little grungy.
A flake leads into a thin crack whose harder middle section takes small cams, then face moves. Above, easier ground on poorer rock runs out to a bolted belay; test holds before weighting them.

Creep right along right-leaning seams on bolts and small cams (offsets are useful), finishing with a sideways slab move protected by a bolt. Then climb straight up a steep face on hard friction past spaced bolts that cannot simply be aided; this friction finish is the most committing section of the route. Belay off a tree on a large ledge.

From the tree, hike up and right through brush toward the upper wall and scramble a 4th-class ramp that cuts back left to a bolt just above eye level below a small roof; build a gear belay. Do not take the loose gully that heads up and right from the ledge — it does not reconnect with the route. The pitch goes right on knobs, then up and right on well-bolted face holds, with a few hard moves above the bolts.
Climb a corner — the most crack climbing on the route — and finish with a short bolted layback. Expect some dirt and large hollow-sounding blocks; test before pulling.

A slabby 5.7 ramp/corner heads left from the belay: one bolt, then a long stretch where the corner is a seam and the only gear is small hidden placements such as a pocket under a bulge. At the end of the corner, clip a bolt and climb a steep bolted face to the belay. On the rappel this pitch jams ropes.
Sustained friction climbing, well bolted through the first half with a few small cams in a short flake; the upper part is easier, solid and more runout to the anchor.

A boulder move about 10 ft off the anchor on an undercling flake reaches the first bolt; a steep juggy face (2 bolts) leads into a flaring corner where the 5.11a moves are, which can be aided on gear at 5.10 A0. Every move protects well. An easier low-angle crack then slabs out onto the top of the wall.

wa_fire_on_the_mountain.notes: Steep, left-leaning corner-and-chimney system with 5.9 climbing low; the crux comes near the top where the crack arches left and turns slightly overhanging, but gear protection is excellent throughout.
Sustained, varied pitch linking a hand crack, featured face holds, and a short rightward hand traverse to an overhanging crack section below a horizontal roof.
Right-facing corner to a giant heather ledge; several similar-looking corners sit nearby, making this a route-finding pitch as much as a climbing one.
Left-trending crack system toward a pedestal; parties have reported some ambiguity near the top, so favor the leftward line rather than the most obvious crack.
Knob-and-fin face climbing (a bit runout, roughly 5.8R) leads into a right-facing corner that gives this pitch its own hard, near-crux moves.
Featured, juggy face climbing to another large heather ledge — a breather before the last two pitches.
Climbs past a gendarme/prow on hand cracks and positive edges to a belay below the final traverse.
A short pitch traversing left across fun flakes to the final heather ledge, where technical climbing ends and the shared Corkscrew scramble to the summit begins.
wa_fire_on_the_mountain.anchor: Gear (heather ledge, top of technical climbing)

wa_free_at_last.notes: Begins on the modern Tatoosh variation, continuing past the standard anchor to a tree belay through dirty terrain.
Clean low-angle V-slot with a thin crack in the back, plus scrambling and corner sequences.
More sustained than pitch 4, multiple cruxes including a roof section and slab climbing.
Hard face climbing past two bolts into a hand/fist crack in a V-slot.

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.notes: Low-angle, sometimes water-polished slab at 5.4-5.8, with runouts that can be long but on easy ground. The first two pitches link in one lead, and a competent party can run the next three and a half as a running belay to the top of the lower slabs. The pitch that reaches the first big ledge can be wet; a ramp on the left avoids it. P7 climbs a short 5.7 wall before easing back to slab. The whole route follows a gully slab, so anything knocked off above funnels straight down these pitches — the many bent hangers show it; do not linger below other parties.

A fun blocky ramp cutting through the steeper wall above the lower slabs, a full rope length from the base of that wall. Protection is sparse — two bolts of 5.7-5.8 at the start, a bolt about halfway and a fixed pin about 15 ft below the belay — but the climbing is easy. On the way down this ramp is downclimbed rather than rappelled.
The first 5.9 pitch, on steeper rock where the bolts are closer together as the moves get harder. It ends on a large ledge.
Easy climbing above the ledge. Skip the chain anchors and scramble to the foot of the steep wall to the left, belaying on a flake below the bolt line of the next pitch.
The first 5.10 pitch: well-bolted, balancy face climbing that is a fair test for the upper crux. Stay on the bolt line; forcing moves off it makes the pitch harder.
A more moderate pitch (roughly 5.8) up to chains. The top of this pitch makes a worthwhile objective on its own; above it the rock and climbing are poorer.

Easy (about 5.0-5.8) but the most runout section, on fair, slightly polished rock that sheds stones onto parties below. P13 is a full rope length with small cams useful in flakes, and can be run as one lead to a second set of chains up and right. A moderate pitch with five or six bolts follows to a belay where the wall kicks back. P15's two bolts are easy to miss and P16-17 have only the stations. Where the wall kicks back, go left to a bolt, up and right to a belay between a stand of trees and a heather patch (about 40 m, two bolts), then right along an obvious ramp of roughly 120 ft to the headwall; the trees and heather are useful landmarks on the descent too. Parties most often get lost here.
The first pitch of the upper headwall, where the bolt line picks back up, finishing on a tricky friction slab (around 5.9).

The crux: a steep, sustained wall nearly a full 60 m rope length, needing around 17 draws (bring long ones or back-clean). Its anchor has no chains; a chained station about 10 m higher lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of this pitch on the descent.
A chimney climbed by stemming and scrounging; it is often wet and can feel harder than the crux late in the day. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
An easier, fun pitch up blocky ground, ending about 30 m below the summit.
A steep friction finish to the summit that looks easy from the belay but has few holds; well bolted and airy. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.

wa_ingalls_peak_friends_in_high_places.notes: Slab traverse with marginal protection (a #0/#0.1 cam helps the first ~20 ft) into the main splitter crack; sustained crack climbing to a ledge belay.
Climbs a corner, then an airy rightward traverse to a large boulder belay on the East Ridge.

wa_kangaroo_temple_north_face.notes: Angled crack then broken rock over ledges past a fixed piton to a 2-bolt rap anchor; take the left or right crack to the final ledge and use long slings to cut rope drag.
Very short ledge traverse right to a shoulder-height block in front of a blind, airy corner; build a gear anchor here before the exposed step-around above.

Exposed step around a blind corner (place a cam low), a tricky step-down, then a flared crack to a tree belay; optionally continue by scrambling or climbing a flake/crack for a short extra pitch to the true summit block, then a short scramble to the summit.

wa_king_kong_gorillas_direct_direct.notes: Start from a small ledge just above the snow on the obvious hand-and-finger splitter. Mantle out the top, pass a tree onto a ledge, then climb a short corner into a chimney and belay above it. The tree has slings around it that are handy for hauling a pack.

Go left up hanging corners around several arêtes, shuffle a short wide section à cheval, then traverse left on slab along an exposed crack. Skip the bolted belay and keep going left on slab through a short face crux to a large slung pillar. Rope drag is severe, so many parties split this pitch.

The Monkey Traverse. Climb the corner of the pillar, then swing right along an exposed horizontal crack to a large sloping ledge. Protect the traverse well for the second and extend placements to manage the rope.

Climb up, then slightly left into a V-slot. Finger cracks and varied stemming weave left, right and left again to the big midway ledge. Here the original Gorillas in the Mist breaks right onto 5.8 ground; King Kong heads left.
Move the belay about 25 ft left to the base of a striking corner crack. A crux start leads into a clean-lined corner and a good belay ledge. This pitch and the next are shared with Gorillas Direct.

A short, stout corner crack ends in a mantle onto a ledge. Continue up the crack onto slab where protection is sparse, traverse right-to-left into another corner crack, and finish with a rightward traverse to a two-pin belay. Back the pins up with small nuts.

Fifth Avenue. Climb the corner and the roof bulge above, move right then left into a stem-box, then go right on steep jugs with spaced protection to a two-bolt anchor at the base of the headwall. Grades given for this pitch range from 5.10b to 5.10+; back up the anchor with small nuts.

The Empire State Building headwall splitter. Slabby cracks and blocks lead to vertical tombstone flakes, then a step left into a hand-and-finger crack and back right into the main splitter. It is sustained hands and fists with powerful laybacking, wide sections and chockstones, with a crux pulling the lip. Graded 5.11d by the first-ascent party and 5.12a on some topos. Two small fixed nuts remain.
A final fifth-class pitch scrambles to the top of the wall. From there most parties descend the West Ridge gullies to Stuart Pass rather than continuing to the summit.

wa_liberty_bell_freedom_rider.notes: Start in the loose corner system roughly 100 ft left of Liberty Crack. Protection is sparse and much of what exists is in suspect rock, so treat it as a runout 5.8; the belay stance at the top is awkward. Test holds and keep the rope out of the loose blocks.

A short stretch of wider crack gives way to thinner climbing above. There is a choice of belays: stop on the broken ledge, or continue to the foot of the offwidth, which is where both P3 options start.

The easier of the two crux options: thin, discontinuous cracks left of the offwidth, balancy and technical, with small and mediocre gear, then a traverse right into a finger crack. Extra small nuts help. It sees less traffic than P3b and is dirtier for it. Choose this OR P3b, not both.

The direct alternative to P3a: an offwidth in the mid-5.10 range that pulls a small roof on a 7-inch-plus crack, then hand stacks into a splitter finger-to-hands crack. Bring cams to 6 in; without the big pieces the offwidth is effectively unprotected. Choose this OR P3a.
An easy hand crack leads to an exposed step left that is far more solid than it looks, then thin cracks finish the pitch. Protect the move left well for the follower.
Steep hand cracks on large crystals, sustained for the grade. The pitch ends on a big ledge with a tree to anchor on, a good place to regroup before the traverse.
Drop down slightly from the ledge and traverse beneath the feature known as the Rotten Block to reach the Liberty Crack line. Stay under the block rather than pulling on it; it earns its name.

The route now shares Liberty Crack's upper pitches for roughly two and a half rope lengths, stopping below Liberty Crack's final 5.9 corner. That ground starts with steep moves off a ledge to a bolt (commonly french-freed; the grade here is the free grade), then goes left through quartz and easier chimneys to a sheltered, treed triangular ledge.
Leave Liberty Crack by traversing right into a thin crack. There are two traverse options, a higher easy one and a lower hard one, and each has a bolt. Can be linked with P11 if rope drag allows.
Mostly an enjoyable hand crack heading toward the chimney above. Belay at the base of the chimney, where there are scattered fixed pins; back them up.
Medusa's Roof: exposed but secure climbing up and around a chockstone at the top of the chimney. The position is the memorable part; the moves are well within the grade of the pitches below.
Climb up and right from the belay into a right-facing corner. It starts simply but thins toward the top, where the feet become smears. Keep something small handy for the upper corner.
Scramble to the summit. The first 50 ft or so is Class 4, after which it is mostly Class 2-3; it can take several rope lengths if belayed throughout. From the summit, use the standard descent.

wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line.notes: Mellow slabbing up discontinuous cracks and bolts; the obvious four-bolt first pitch that ends at a set of chains is the standard orientation landmark for the route.
Easy initial moves to a small roof where insecure lie-backing provides the pitch's tricky bit, then easier ground to a gear belay below a roof-capped dihedral.
Sustained stemming and lie-backs up a beautiful corner; a sometimes-wet, wild crux move gains the roof before exiting left to bolts.
Move up and left to the roof lip, clip two bolts, then traverse right on a flake to a stance and bolted anchor.
A beautiful, techy rightward traverse on perfect stone accesses a left-facing corner; technical stemming through four bolts with a slight crux move to a good hold.

The route's benchmark crux: climb the corner to a small roof, step right into a hanging finger crack, then a bouldery crux between two seams before easing off on a mellow finger crack. This is the pitch freed by Kate Rutherford and Mikey Schaefer in 2008 to complete the free line at 5.12c.
Moderate crack climbing leads up and right to a two-bolt anchor on a large ledge system.
Thin, technical moves on more perfect rock protected by small gear and fixed heads/pitons; the last hard pitch before easier ground.
Engaging corner climbing with a brief thin move, then a mantle onto M&M Ledge, the mid-height junction shared with Live Free or Die and other East Face lines.
Easier corner and ledge climbing above M&M Ledge, working up the upper apron toward the summit block on golden, lower-angle granite.
Rad, easy scrambling atop Liberty Bell to the true summit; most parties instead rappel from M&M Ledge (four double-rope raps via bolts) rather than finish this far.

wa_liberty_crack.notes: A right-facing corner then a splitter crack lead straight up to a clean bolted belay shortly below the Lithuanian Lip; some parties aid/hybrid this pitch.

The historic Lithuanian Lip: go up and out the roof, get over the top, then aid a bolt ladder (or free climb it at 5.13- for strong parties) to a bolted belay. Most parties aid this section for the route's standard 5.11a grade.
Face climbing or aid with fixed heads leads to a crack and old pitons, ending at a bolted anchor; freeing is fastest from here upward.
Jam a nice crack that hardens from 5.8 to 5.10 as it goes, ending at another bolted belay.
Continue upward along a corner system to another bolted belay; a relatively relaxed pitch between harder sections.
Mostly easy stemming (mind loose rock) leads to a brief crux surmounting a big block, protected by a single shiny bolt, to bolted anchors.
Steep moves off the belay gain a ramp/corner with a long-runner bolt and 5.10- moves over an overlap to a decent seat; belay is built from pitons and small cams.
Go up and left through fun quartz features then 5.6 chimneys to a triangular ledge with a finger-crack gear anchor.
A long, excellent pitch up a left-facing corner and slab with beautiful moments of exposure over the East Face; belay off a large tree.
Continue up easy terrain until reaching sandy ledges; a rappel anchor is available nearby in case a party strays onto the wrong terrain.
Third-class ledges allow unroping or simul-climbing toward the summit shoulder alcove.
Easy terrain leads to the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder, the start of the standard two-rappel descent into Beckey Gully shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider, and the Beckey Route.

wa_live_free_or_die.notes: Clean face climbing past several bolts and V2-V3-ish overlaps; mostly on-your-feet bolted climbing low on the East Face.
Continuation of bolted slab climbing past more overlaps in the same clean-face style as P1.
Easy-to-follow, mostly bolted face climbing to a bolted pedestal belay beneath a broad roof, just left of the Independence Route's quartz chimney.

The route's namesake crux: a sideways, height-dependent downclimb-dyno roughly partway up the pitch, crimpy and reachy, with bolt protection backing up the pendulum; finishes on excellent 5.10-5.11+ face climbing. Established via toprope over six weeks by Herrington, Hadley, and Keena-Levin in summer 2017.
Step right onto a mostly bolted pitch ending with a delicate V3 mantle to a tiny stance; protection mixes bolts, gear, and old pitons in the overlaps.
A height-dependent V4 move gains a flake, then a thin crack system takes small gear up to a nice ledge below a massive roof.
Climb left past a bolt through the roof, then 5.9 cracks lead to a bolted traverse heading left, then back-clean the leftmost bolt on the way across.
Splitter hand cracks lead to M&M Ledge, the shared mid-height junction with Thin Red Line, where most parties either rappel or continue up Thin Red Line's finish to the summit.

Above the ledge the last three pitches to the top follow the finishing section of the neighbouring 5.8 line, which is where nearly every party finishes. Easy, low-angle climbing to the summit; a splitter crack beginning about 35 m above the ledge is the best of it.

wa_miracle_ramps.notes: Horizontal crack, hogback ridges, diagonal cracks; smear past four bolts to a trough - the route's crux.
Smearing and knobs rightward past three bolts, thin crack, knobby climbing to an anchor above a flake.
'Ruffled Crack' undercling, rightward edges, friction moves to a good vertical crack and a ledge.
Friction and edges to two bolts, overlap climbing, a bolted seam.
Three bolts to a wide crack, flake traverse, three more bolts on slab to fractured cracks.
Cracks and blocks, a slanting overlap system, flake layback, three bolts to the summit anchor.

wa_mount_stuart_girth_pillar.notes: Rope up for the access ramp off the lower North Ridge onto the upper Ice Cliff Glacier; belay off pickets or rock gear as terrain dictates.
Continue up moderate glacier-margin rock, staying alert to icefall from the ice cliff above.
Cross benches toward the base of the pillar; the 'ice cliff' step itself (10-100+ ft of 50-70° snow/ice) is passed nearby depending on the season's line.
Final easy pitch reaching the actual base of the Girth Pillar proper around 8,200-8,400 ft.
A nice but immediately steep hand crack that jogs right at the top; belay on a crappy, tiny ledge.
Shuffle left about 10 feet to a thin crack; finger jams lead to a rest right before the crux, protected by a fixed stopper, then thin hands to a hand crack and a better belay.
Perfect hands on very steep, somewhat dirty rock lead to the top of the pillar; beware some very large loose blocks.
Easier crack and face climbing off the top of the pillar toward the upper glacier basin.
Continued moderate rock leading toward the false summit above the Ice Cliff Glacier.
Broken, easier terrain closing in on the false summit.

Easy scrambling to the main false summit above the Ice Cliff Glacier, joining Stuart's standard upper North Ridge/summit terrain; there is no reasonable way to reverse the route given the glacier's icefall hazard below.

wa_news_nw_corner.notes: 45m crack/corner topped by a short, poorly protected chimney section; easy climbing gains a broad, tree-covered ledge used as the first belay.
50m up and left, weaving through trees (and often lingering snow patches) and a corner to reach a second belay ledge; sustained but moderate climbing.
30m up a left-leading flake and wide crack requiring big cams (bring the #4-#5!); committing 5.9 liebacks lead to a belay slung around a small rock pillar.
25m of surprisingly secure offwidth: smear the face while arm-barring the crack for balance. Widely cited as the burly technical crux, ending at a sloping ledge below a roof.
30m traverse left around the roof (watch rope drag), then easing cracks lead directly to the summit; low 4th class scrambling to finish.

wa_north_face_3.notes: Crux of the route right off the ground: an awkward rightward-trending handcrack, easing above to a large belay block slung with tat.
Blocky, mossy terrain wandering back and forth, trending right, to belay at the notch between the true and west summits.

Many parties unrope here and scramble the exposed 'Stegosaur' ridge crest to the true summit; those staying roped must re-lead on the way down since this pitch is a traverse and cannot be rappelled directly.

wa_northwest_arete.notes: From the notch, descend briefly then climb back up through trees and over blocks; loose in spots right at the start near the bivy sites.
Ascend a right-facing corner to reach easy ground and a good stance at the base of a steeper face.
Diagonal traverse up and rightward across ledges, then straight up to a good ledge system; belayer needs to reposition left along the ledge to manage rope drag.
An easy ramp leads up and right into one tricky move, then easier traversing terrain to the highest large ledge on the route.
The best pitch on the route: a steep, well-protected corner with good holds, ending below another right-facing corner.
Diagonal traverse on easier ground to a flake requiring an au cheval (straddle) move, followed by one insecure, tricky move up to a good ledge — the route's technical crux.
Two corner options at the top; the right-hand corner is the mellower choice, but resist the urge to beeline for the skyline — traverse left off it to reach the summit ridge cleanly.

wa_princely_ambitions.notes: Left up easy flake/ramp, past one bolt on face, more flakes, chalked ledge traverses left, then straight up corner to belay (longest/best pitch).
Big flake left of anchor, right-facing dihedral/crack, bulge to climb over, finishes on dirty wide crack to rap station.

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.notes: A right-leaning crack system leads to the obvious roof; it is hard to miss. Most parties find this the hardest-feeling pitch, though the technical crux comes later. Fingertip to hand-size gear, doubles recommended.

Move out right beneath the roof and take the corner above it. The move under the roof is the technical crux and a small cam (a purple C3 was useful) protects it. The pitch ends at a long horizontal crack that takes a #3-size cam, where you belay on gear while standing in the crack. Parties often link this with the first half of the next pitch, or stop at a stance in the corner after linking pitch 1.

A slab leads to a short chimney exit. The chimney has loose rock, so one option is to skip it: take the ramp to its right and traverse left over the top into the easy corner. If you do climb it, follow the seam arcing left on the chimney's left wall. Linking this with the 5.8 above reaches a belay on a large ledge, and a 60 m rope often forces a stop before the looser 5.8 section.
Off-width to a mantle on an arching seam, ending on the large ledge at the foot of the last pitch. Often climbed together with pitch 3, in which case a 70 m rope links it more easily.

The aesthetic finishing corner: a perfect corner crack above the ledge, about 50 feet, with small gear and nuts useful at the start (tips to fingers), then move right to a little tree just under the West Ridge crest. With enough gear and good rope management you can carry on to the top of the ridge, then either rappel the back side or continue to the summit. Some rate this pitch softer than the earlier 5.11a.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.notes: Wide crack (a #4 cam protects the crux size) and low fifth-class terrain up to trees; often combined with pitch 2.
Crack climbing exiting right on knobs, belaying at the highest trees before the gully.
Sustained gully climbing, belaying just below an obvious chockstone.
Steep double cracks lead to a tunnel behind the giant chockstone; belay at the top or in the squeeze chimney.
The flaring squeeze chimney crux — demanding for many parties, knee protection is useful; belay above on a ledge.
The 'amazing left-facing corner' pitch, sustained stemming on knobs, straight to the summit.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes: Long pitch from the overhanging rock at the base, reached by scrambling east from Prusik Pass: blocky climbing up a distinct crack onto the West Ridge crest, belaying where the ridge levels off.
Follow the flat trail around the north side, then climb 15 ft to the south side for great exposure; belay at a slingable block just before the crux slab.
The crux friction slab pitch, protected by an old fixed pin; back onto the south side for more exposure, then drop to the north side and traverse to the last-pitch ledge.
Two finishing options: a finger crack with fun face moves protected by a bolt hidden behind a bulge, or a 5.7 off-width/layback with hand jams (nuts + a 0.75 cam) through a final squeeze chimney.

wa_sews_sw_rib.notes: From the Y-larch, cracks through an awkward bulge (~160 ft) to a ledge below the Wavy Crack; widely cited as the route's technical crux.
The wide left-leaning Wavy Crack (~80 ft) to a tree belay.
Up and left to a tree, then up and right below the Boving Roof (~60 ft) to a gear belay.
Right around the corner past delicate unprotected slab to the base of dual offwidths (~100 ft).
The Bear Hug dual-offwidth pitch (~80 ft), then up and right to a strenuous corner belay.
Clip a bolt for pro, easy slab to a runout arete, belay at the Rabbit Ears towers (~165 ft).
Rappel or downclimb into the gully, then easy cracks to the summit blocks (~80 ft).

wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.notes: Skirts the ridge on its climber's-right side across large blocks, then follows a short dihedral to the crest for the belay, onto the north face before reaching the notch at the base of the steep south-facing ridge; solid, featured granite throughout.

Continues up the exposed crest on solid rock with good gear, staying a few feet left of the crest; passes an old fixed rappel anchor about 30 ft below where the ridge steepens into a layback. It is graded 5.0, but several parties feel it climbs nearer 5.4, harder and more awkward than the route's nominal grade, making it the pitch most people remember.
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.anchor: Gear (near an old fixed rap anchor)

wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.notes: Combines the route's final rope-lengths: moderate class-4/low-5th climbing at or just right of the crest through the summit blocks, finishing with a few reachy, exposed moves to the small, airy summit (8,120 ft) with views into the Ptarmigan Traverse country.

wa_southeast_face.notes: The route's best and hardest pitch: delicate face moves into a thin crack, climbed high above the Boston Glacier and its open crevasses; sustained and the technical crux of the tower. There is no anchor at the very base, so the belayer must stay attentive on that stretch.
wa_southeast_face.anchor: Gear (thin crack/face pro); no anchor at the very base of the pitch

wa_southeast_face.notes: Dirtier and less straightforward route-finding than pitch 1, following crack and face features to a sparse two-bolt anchor; this sparse station (no chains or rap rings) starts the pair of ~23m rappels back down to the Southeast Ridge notch.
wa_southeast_face.anchor: 2-bolt anchor (no chains/rings - leave a locking biner or cord)

wa_spontaneous_distraction.notes: The first bolt blends into the rock and is hard to spot. Climb just above a left-trending overlap, then up past three bolts on thin, exciting face climbing to the anchor. Short runouts, and some poor rock between bolts.

Climb past two bolts to reach a crack. At the third bolt, traverse right and follow easier cracks to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can each be rappelled with a 70 m rope. Short runouts and some poor rock.

The long bolted pitch. A hard start for about the first 20 ft, then moderate 5.7–5.8 face and slab climbing to a tree anchor. The webbing at the tree may need replacing, so inspect it before trusting it.

Enjoyable cracks graded 5.6–5.7 lead to the top. Belay from a gear anchor or a tree. To descend, scramble back to the top of pitch 3 and rappel the route. A standard rack to 2 inches works, with extra runners for rope drag.

wa_starfish_enterprise.notes: Start about 50 ft left of Good Girls Like Bad Boys at a two-bolt stance on a narrow part of Madsen's Ledge (a hand line has been in place). Face and arete past three bolts reach a steep corner with a crack in the back; stem and jam it on cams, then a tricky arete and more stemming lead to a semi-hanging belay.
Head left from the belay to join the second pitch of Good Girls Like Bad Boys above that pitch's crux. Pitches 1 and 2 can be linked with little rope drag.
Climb the excellent third pitch of Good Girls Like Bad Boys, the corner line, to a belay in the corner.
Leave the corner and move left onto the exposed face for a long, varied pitch. Watch the feet around the starfish-shaped feature the route is named for.
A tenuous move just above the belay is the hard part; above it, climb broken face past bolts. A few small cams help protect the easier ground between bolts. Descend as for Good Girls Like Bad Boys.

wa_technicians_of_the_sacred.notes: The striking black-and-white streaked open corner right of Swim and Green Dragon, almost directly above where the trail reaches the wall. Tricky steep moves low in the corner lead into pumpy overhanging climbing on sloping edges and pockets; the hardest section is short, then angle and difficulty ease toward the ledge anchor. Often wet from the waterfall until summer.
A bolted ramp. Grades given range from 5.11- to 5.11b. Bolts on the upper wall vary in age, and many belays are sling anchors, so carry webbing to back up or replace faded tat.
A low-angle face with sparse bolts; grades given are 5.12- to 5.12a. Supplement or replace old webbing at the belay as needed.

The pitch through the Golden Arch. The usual way climbs about 8 ft higher up the corner to an obvious finger-bucket rail that leads back right to the arete (5.11b), then up corners above. A harder direct option takes the arete straight on at about 5.12b/c. Rappelling back over this arete leaves the rappeller hanging in space.
Continuous climbing through corners and aretes, given as 5.11 to 5.11b. Steep and featured, with big holds, high heel hooks and technical stemming; one of the best pitches on the upper wall.
The only unbolted pitch: a hand crack that needs natural gear. Carry a light rack of hand-size cams for it; everything below is bolt-protected.

wa_the_cave_route.notes: Starting about 50 ft down the gully from the notch, climb two semi-parallel diagonal cracks past a dead tree, then traverse right to the belay. Recent reports say the belay tree may no longer be there, so rack extra gear to build an anchor. Loose, variable ('oatmeal') rock in spots demands care with hand and foot placements.
wa_the_cave_route.anchor: Tree/gear (belay tree reported gone — build anchor)

wa_the_cave_route.notes: Traverse left beneath an overhang and around a corner to the mouth of 'the cave' (sling belay), then move through the cave itself — roughly 20 ft of traversing/squeezing — to a second belay at the far end. Bring a few extender slings or rope drag becomes a serious problem through this section.

A moderate 5.4 crack, entered via a knobby slab on the left or a short lieback, eases into easy face climbing to a tree belay; from there it's an exposed, unroped 40 ft scramble to the small summit, so consider keeping the rope on for less confident parties.

wa_the_velvet_pedestal.notes: Blocky corner cleaning up higher; intermediate chained anchor ~50ft; two 5.9 crack options to a sloping ledge belay.
Traverse left on slab below bolt, then cracks past second bolt to small overlap, left to ledge with chained anchor.
Multiple finish options: crack pair to ramp/corner, or lower belay for laybacking/stemming, undercling, or face-crack finish.

wa_the_tooth_south_face.notes: From Pineapple Pass, climb up and trend right through the main groove/line of weakness on solid, juggy andesite. The small tree historically used for the belay at the top of this pitch is dead and sketchy, so sling a solid horn or block instead.
Climb right onto a ledge and follow connecting ledges back and forth (several sub-variations exist) to a stance near a pair of trees on the left, which serve as the rappel anchor for the descent.
An easy, low-angle scramble up short steps and connecting ledges (choose-your-own-adventure terrain, path of least resistance trends right) leads to a belay stance below the final steep headwall.

The technical crux, with three finish options: most parties go slightly right up a juggy right-facing flake (5.3); a steeper splitter crack (5.8) exits further left for harder climbing; the classic line continues left on balancey, exposed 5.4 moves across the narrow 'Catwalk' ledge before an unroped scramble tops out on the summit block.

wa_this_my_friend.notes: Fifty feet of easy climbing and a face move around a recessed pod lead into the main crack system; this pitch is credited with the route's overall 5.10a rating even though individual-pitch consensus lists it as 5.9+.
Stem past a 10-foot offwidth pod before launching into a gorgeous, sustained hand-jamming corner crack.
A broken crack system gains a sloping ledge below a pair of obvious zig-zag cracks; belay on a wide, sandy ledge.
A clean headwall splitter crack offers phenomenal, varied jamming; move left along a thin rail to gain the main crack, finishing on a large flat ledge.
Climb up and left through broken ledges and face features to a belay alcove below the summit pinnacle; the route is explicitly not set up for rappel, so descend on foot from here.

wa_the_west_face.notes: Shared with the Northwest Corner; dirty face/chimney with trees to a huge sandy ledge at the base of a large corner. ~160 ft.
Steep right-facing corner with good cracks and gear to a belay ledge. ~60 ft.
Low-angle crack to a lieback flake, airy step right past a bolt, sustained undercling/lieback into a corner crack. ~90 ft.
The crux: a thin tips crack, then a step left into easier climbing; a hanging belay option exists higher up. ~150 ft.
Low-angle crack climbing with a friction-slab traverse right to the top or a bolted anchor. ~150 ft.

wa_west_ridge_2.notes: Start up the white-streaked, S-shaped crack that passes a tree; the 5.8 is a few face moves about halfway up, and the pitch belays on a ledge just left of the crest. Above, easy fifth-class blocks and some tree-thrashing lead along the ridge to a big ledge beside a boulder. With a long rope the two pitches link; the lower crack seeps and can be wet.

A sustained splitter hand crack on excellent rock climbs to a tree; from there move right and continue to the next ledge. The belay is built on gear (a #1 cam fits at the stance). Some rate the crack closer to 5.8 for how long it keeps going.

The technical crux: a steep, awkward pair of parallel cracks that flare into a short dihedral. It is pumpy but there are rests, and small cams protect it well. Grades given range from 5.8 to 5.9-. After the cracks, traverse left onto the face to a ledge with a tree belay; long slings help, as rope drag builds from the traverse.

Climb back up from the tree to regain the ridge. The more direct line starts with a hard layback and eases quickly but is sparsely protected; the alternative is a short, awkward fourth-class traverse that adds rope drag. Easy fourth class then leads to a belay at the base of the next splitter.

Follow the 5.6 splitter up mostly fourth-class ridge, then make an exposed traverse around the right side of a gendarme. Rope drag is the main problem on this long pitch: extend placements before the traverse, or stop short of the gendarme if the rope is dragging badly.
Stem and jam straight up a pair of parallel cracks, taking solid gear, to a good belay ledge below the final wall. A clean, enjoyable pitch that sets up the widening crack of the last lead.

A crack that widens to 4–6 inches leads to left-trending, exposed 5.8 face moves on a blank slab before reaching a jug and the ridge top. The face section is widely treated as the mental crux: protection is small and sparse, so carry wires and the smallest cams (a 0.2-size cam is valuable here) and climb it carefully.

wa_wright_pond.notes: 55m. Climb the obvious left-facing arch into a corner with a strenuous pinch-move crux to a bolted belay at a ledge.
50m. Ascend a large flake into an open book with stemming and thin finger work, then traverse bolted face climbing on small edges and pockets to a bolted belay.
50m. Technical right-facing corner transitions into left-facing crack work, finishing at a treed ledge belay.
45m. Blocky corner/chimney leads to low-angle slab and a hand/fist crack exit.
